events.title: The death of St. Servulus
events.shortBlurb: The palsied beggar of St. Clement's porch, who had never been able to stand or to lift his hand to his mouth, died singing psalms about the year 590…
body: St. Gregory the Great, who preserves his memory in the Dialogues and in a homily to his people, presents Servulus as the very figure of Lazarus in the Gospel: a beggar afflicted with the palsy from his infancy, never able to stand, to sit upright, to lift his hand to his mouth, or to turn himself from one side to another.

His mother and brother carried him into the porch of St. Clement's church at Rome, where he lived on the alms of those that passed by and shared what he could spare with other needy persons. He entreated the devout to read the holy Scriptures to him, and heard them so attentively that he learned them by heart, and consecrated his days to singing hymns of praise and thanksgiving.

When his sickness seized his vitals and he felt his end draw near, he desired the poor and pilgrims who had often shared his charity to sing sacred psalms beside him; then, of a sudden, he cried, 'Silence! Do you not hear the sweet melody which resounds in the heavens?' and so expired, about the year 590. He was buried in St. Clement's church, where his tomb was honoured with miracles, as the Roman Martyrology records.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 December
